name: Bandhan-Konnagar (charityevals)
summary: Bandhan-Konnagar, a non-profit society in Kolkata, runs Targeting the Hardcore Poor, a graduation programme for ultra-poor women-headed households in 16 Indian states (an asset, a weekly stipend and 24 months of coaching), and smaller health, education, skills, financial literacy and farming programmes, and advises Bihar's government graduation programme. Against its fiscal year 2024-25 spending (US$13.9M with overhead, 11,201 households enrolled), the randomized trial of its own programme in West Bengal, where participants' consumption was 22% to 56% above the control group's over ten years, gives about 6 years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainties are how well that small 2007 trial carries to today's programme (a large trial of Bihar's version supports it) and how long the gain lasts after year ten; the accounts give no split by programme, so each programme's share of the spending is a judgment. The health, education, skills, financial literacy, farming and Bihar branches, about 5% of the result, are discounted for missing data.

rows.explainer: The accounts give no split by programme. Our judgment from the grants received for each programme in the year and its staff: About ₹53 crore of the ₹98 crore: the grants given only for this programme in the year (ITC ₹11.7 crore and three foreign foundations ₹69.1 crore, receipts and payments account, printed p. 61), Bandhan Bank's ₹6.26 crore for it (bank annual report p. 95) and a quarter of Bajaj Finance's ₹11.1 crore (it funds four programmes, donor table p. 51), less the ₹36.2 crore rise in unspent grants over the year (balance sheet p. 59), most of it the foundation grants received in December 2024 and March 2025. rows.label: Yearly fade of the gain after year 10
rows.explainer: The trial's gain grew to year 7 and was still 34% of control consumption for participants at year 10, with no sign of the control group catching up (p. 13). Beyond that nothing is measured. Our judgment: 10% a year, 0 (the trial's 7-to-10-year path, where most of the gain held) to 30% (Ethiopia's graduation pilot, where control households caught up by year 7, as the Bihar paper notes, p. 2).

rows.label: Years the gain lasts after year 10
rows.explainer: Our judgment, 10 years (0 to 20): the recipients were a median 44 years old at the start (p. 5), so the household's gain from the asset and the new work lasts into their 60s; 0 if the year-10 gain is the last.

rows.label: Total ln(consumption) gain per person, present value
rows.formula: (thp_g_18m * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, thp_years_18m) + thp_g_3y * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, thp_years_3y) / (1 + $discount_rate) ^ thp_years_18m + thp_g_7y * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, thp_years_7y) / (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (thp_years_18m + thp_years_3y) + thp_g_10y * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, thp_years_10y) / (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (thp_years_18m + thp_years_3y + thp_years_7y) + thp_g_10y * pv_annuity_due(1, (1 + $discount_rate) / (1 - fade_rate) - 1, tail_years) / (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (thp_years_18m + thp_years_3y + thp_years_7y + thp_years_10y)) * thp_evidence_adj * thp_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Each survey's gain over the years it stands for, discounted at the shared rate, then the year-10 gain fading after year 10; times the programme's evidence and missing-data steps.

rows.label: Spillover benefits to non-participants, as a share of participants' benefits
rows.explainer: Not measured: the trial randomized households within hamlets, so effects on neighbours are invisible (and, if positive, make the control group better off, lowering the estimate). The Bihar trial randomized whole village councils and found larger effects (0.38-0.44 SD against 0.29-0.31 SD in West Bengal, Bihar paper p. 9), consistent with small positive local effects. Our judgment 5%, 0 to 30%.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of consumption benefits
rows.explainer: Neither trial measured deaths, so 0, as the template asks; the high end allows for a child-mortality effect of a 20-50% consumption rise. The adults' measured health gain is in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Baseline monthly consumption per person, trial households (2018 PPP $)

source.title: Banerjee, Duflo and Sharma, 'Long-term Effects of the Targeting the Ultra Poor Program', NBER Working Paper 28074 (2020; published in American Economic Review: Insights 3(4), 2021)
source.quote: They had monthly per capita consumption of $40 (2018 USD PPP) and owned less than 0.1 acres of land.

rows.explainer: Context: about US$1.35 a day per person at 2018 purchasing-power parity before the programme. Each survey's gain is taken against that survey's control mean (thp_ctrl_*), which rose with India's growth, not against this baseline, so the gains are not overstated.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, Targeting the Hardcore Poor
rows.explainer: Internal validity about 0.9: a pre-registered randomized trial of Bandhan's own programme, attrition balanced across arms (p. 6), but only 978 households and wide intervals at year 10. Dividing by take-up assumes the 48% who refused were unaffected and that the effect on the 52% who joined speaks for today's participants: about 0.9. Carry to today's programme in 16 states with 24 months of coaching (the trial: Murshidabad, 18 months, 2007) about 0.95: the at-scale randomized trial of Bihar's government version, which Bandhan-Konnagar designed and supports, found consumption 27-30% above the control mean two and three years on (Bihar paper, abstract), as large as the West Bengal trial's effect on participants at the same horizons. 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.95 ≈ 0.75, 0.5 to 0.95.

rows.label: Missing-data step, Targeting the Hardcore Poor
rows.explainer: Measured (templates.md Convention 12): Bandhan-Konnagar's own count of households enrolled meets a randomized trial of its own programme, delivered the same way (asset, stipend, coaching to the same women-headed ultra-poor households), with the at-scale Bihar trial as support.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The trial's effect is already net of its control group, who got what they would have got anyway in 2007-2017. Today India's rural livelihoods mission runs its own graduation schemes in some states (Bihar's Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana, below), so some households Bandhan-Konnagar enrols might later be reached by one. Our judgment 0.9, 0.75 to 1.

rows.label: Bandhan-Konnagar's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Bandhan-Konnagar buys the assets, pays the stipend and employs the coaches (912 staff). Others' resources: village committees that help select households, government officials who issue identity documents and entitlements the coaches link households to, and J-PAL's monitoring. Our judgment 0.95, 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of counted households that get the programme as studied
rows.explainer: The count is Bandhan-Konnagar's own, without outside verification. It reports 185,096 of its 198,081 households since 2006 as graduated (93%, p. 9); some of the rest are still in the programme. Our judgment 0.95, 0.85 to 1.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Bandhan-Konnagar has large reserves of its own (₹543 crore corpus, balance sheet p. 59), funds its schools and administration from their income, and gets a share of the Bandhan group's legally required corporate social responsibility spending. A gift for its programmes is spent on them (unspent grants are held separately), but some of it may free group money for other uses. Our judgment 0.95, 0.8 to 1.05.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Each effect not modelled, with its sign: adults' physical health (+0.19 SD at year 10) and mental health (+0.20 SD) in the West Bengal trial (Table 1), and +1.35 SD in mental health in Bihar's (abstract), not counted in consumption: +5% to +15%; women's say in the household and political participation: small and positive; assets still held after the consumption gain ends: in the tail; harms (debt taken on, animals lost, effort of the women's new work, which consumption does not net out): -5%. rows.label: Evidence adjustment, health programme
rows.explainer: The trials' packages were intensive (trained workers' home visits around birth, women's groups meeting monthly) and mostly from settings where most births were at home; Bandhan's volunteers run health forums, counsel at the doorstep, sell health products and escort women to government facilities (pp. 15-16). Our judgment 0.4 of the trials' effect, 0.15 to 0.7.

rows.label: Share of the health outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Every Indian village has a government community health worker (ASHA) doing much of the same counselling, and most births are now in facilities; the trials' control groups had far less. Our judgment: half of the effect is beyond what women would get anyway, 25% to 80%.

rows.label: Bandhan-Konnagar's share of the resources behind the health outcome
rows.explainer: Unpaid volunteers' time (13,274 Swasthya Sahayikas trained since the start) and the government clinics the programme refers women to. Our judgment 0.8, 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Missing-data step, health programme
rows.explainer: Thin: the reach is partly judged and the effect comes from trials of other, more intensive delivery; no controlled evaluation of this programme. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Newborn deaths averted by the health programme
rows.formula: hp_households * @household_size.india * rural_cbr / 1000 * nmr / 1000 * (1 - hp_rr) * hp_evidence_adj * hp_counterfactual_adj
rows.explainer: Households served × people per household (@household_size.india) × births per person × neonatal deaths per birth × the share averted.

rows.label: Units of value from the health programme
rows.explainer: Deaths valued at the shared value of a newborn's death; illness averted and the 25 water treatment plants are not counted (small next to the deaths).

rows.label: New education programme students in fiscal year 2024-25

source.title: Bandhan-Konnagar, Annual Report 2024-25, with the audited financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 (JSUS & Associates)
source.note: Cumulative at the end of each fiscal year; 150,162 - 145,933 = 4,229 new in 2024-25.

rows.explainer: The annual report says its programme figures other than states and staff are cumulative (p. 8), and Bandhan Bank calls its part of the same count cumulative outreach (bank annual report p. 96), so the year's rise is new students. Children who joined Bandhan Education Centres (free remedial centres run by trained local women) and Bandhan Academies (low-fee primary schools) in the year, Bandhan-Konnagar's count.

rows.label: Years a child stays in a centre or academy
rows.explainer: The centres take children of 4 to 6 years and support them through the first grades of primary school (p. 20); academies teach up to class 5. Our judgment 3 years, 2 to 5.

rows.label: Students in the three Bandhan Schools, academic year 2024-25

source.title: Bandhan-Konnagar, Annual Report 2024-25, with the audited financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 (JSUS & Associates)
source.quote: Total number of students during the academic year 2024-25 635 415 230

rows.explainer: Aranghata 635, Taldi 415, Chakdaha 230: English-medium schools following the national CBSE curriculum.

rows.label: Children taught in the year
Test-score gain per child per year of remedial teaching (standard deviations)

source.title: Banerjee, Cole, Duflo and Linden, 'Remedying Education: Evidence from Two Randomized Experiments in India', Quarterly Journal of Economics 122(3), 2007, pp. 1235-1264
source.quote: It increased average test scores of all children in treatment schools by 0.28 standard deviation

rows.explainer: Pratham's remedial programme, which hired young local women to teach children lagging behind, raised scores 0.28 SD over two years: 0.14 a year. 0.05 (the academies, low-fee schools whose gains over government schools are small in India) to 0.28.

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of a childhood learning gain
rows.explainer: The site's figures: 20% more earnings per SD of adult skill × 40% of a programme's gain lasting to adulthood.

rows.label: Years until the children start work
rows.explainer: Children of 4 to 10 start work at about 16 to 20. Our judgment 12 years, 8 to 15.

rows.label: Earnings gain per child, ln(consumption), present value
rows.explainer: The yearly gain in log earnings over the shared working life, after the wait, discounted, shared with the household (@givewell_shared.resource_sharing_multiplier), as the site's other education models do.

rows.label: Share of the education outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The children are in government schools anyway; many families would otherwise pay for private tuition, which the centres aim to replace (p. 20). Our judgment 0.7, 0.4 to 0.9.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education
rows.explainer: One urban trial of a similar remedial model, carried to rural centres for younger children run by another organisation. Our judgment 0.6, 0.3 to 0.9.

rows.label: Bandhan-Konnagar's share of the resources behind the education outcome
rows.explainer: Parents pay fees at the academies and schools, and the government schools teach the same children. Our judgment 0.85, 0.7 to 1.

rows.label: Missing-data step, education
rows.explainer: Thin: no controlled evaluation of these centres; the effect is from another programme's trial and the reach partly judged.

rows.label: Units of value from education
rows.formula: ed_students * ed_ln_gain * $uov_per_ln_consumption * ed_counterfactual_adj * ed_evidence_adj * ed_attribution_share * ed_missing_data_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount

source.note: Cumulative at the end of each fiscal year; 43,608 - 39,917 = 3,691 placed in 2024-25.

rows.explainer: Bandhan-Konnagar's count of trainees from its skill centres placed in jobs in the year.

rows.label: Share of trainees placed in jobs

source.title: Bandhan-Konnagar, Annual Report 2024-25, with the audited financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 (JSUS & Associates)
source.quote: More than 70% of the trained youth are successfully placed in many renowned companies/industries.

rows.explainer: Bandhan-Konnagar's own figure; Bandhan Bank's assessment found 85% of its centres' trainees found a first job (bank annual report p. 97). 60% to 85%.

rows.label: Young people trained in the year
Earnings gain per trainee from vocational training

source.title: McKenzie, 'How Effective Are Active Labor Market Policies in Developing Countries? A Critical Review of Recent Evidence', World Bank Research Observer 32(2), 2017, pp. 127-154
source.quote: Many of these evaluations find no significant impacts on either employment or earnings.

rows.explainer: Randomized trials of vocational training in developing countries mostly find small effects on earnings; our reading 5%, 0 to 15%, against what trainees would earn anyway (most would find some work).

rows.label: Years skills trainees stay ahead of untrained peers
rows.explainer: Our judgment 5 years, 2 to 10: skills for a first job in retail, logistics or call centres matter less as workers gain experience.

rows.label: Earnings gain per trainee, ln(consumption), present value
rows.explainer: Shared with the household as the site's other later-income models do.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, skills training
rows.explainer: The effect is a reading of other programmes' trials, in other countries. Our judgment 0.8, 0.5 to 1.

rows.label: Bandhan-Konnagar's share of the resources behind the skills outcome
rows.explainer: Employers give on-the-job training, and Bihar's skill mission pays for some courses. Our judgment 0.8, 0.6 to 1.

rows.label: Missing-data step, skills training
rows.explainer: Thin: no controlled evaluation of these centres; the trainee count is derived from placements.

rows.label: Units of value from skills training
rows.formula: eu_trainees * eu_ln_gain * $uov_per_ln_consumption * eu_evidence_adj * eu_attribution_share * eu_missing_data_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount

rows.label: Women taught in the financial literacy programme in fiscal year 2024-25

source.title: Bandhan-Konnagar, Annual Report 2024-25, with the audited financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 (JSUS & Associates)
source.note: Cumulative at the end of each fiscal year; 1,372,954 - 1,247,822 = 125,132 in 2024-25.

rows.explainer: Bandhan-Konnagar's count of women taught by its local educators in the year.

rows.label: Household consumption gain from financial literacy training
rows.explainer: Financial education changes saving and borrowing behaviour a little (a tenth of a standard deviation in the meta-analyses) with little evidence of effects on consumption or income. Our judgment 0.5%, 0 to 2%.

rows.label: Years financial literacy graduates keep their new money habits
rows.explainer: Habits from a short course fade as the educators move on to other villages: our judgment 2 years, 1 (the course year only) to 4 (savings habits and new accounts that stay in use).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, financial literacy
rows.explainer: Self-reported behaviour change in the literature; publication bias. Our judgment 0.7, 0.4 to 1.

rows.label: Missing-data step, financial literacy
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome data for this programme; the gain is a judgment.

rows.label: Units of value from financial literacy
rows.formula: fl_new * @household_size.india * ln(1 + fl_consumption_gain) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, fl_years) * $uov_per_ln_consumption * fl_evidence_adj * fl_missing_data_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount
rows.explainer: Women taught in the year × people per household (@household_size.india) × the gain over its years.

rows.label: Farmers and entrepreneurs supported in the year (climate action and sustainable livelihoods)
rows.explainer: The climate action programme counts 1,409 beneficiaries since 2021 (p. 37) and the sustainable livelihoods programme 116 entrepreneurs graduated (p. 29), 131 by March 2025 (p. 30): about 350 and 50 a year. Our judgment 450, 250 to 1,000.

rows.label: Household consumption gain from farming support or business training
rows.explainer: Seeds, farmer field schools and new crops (dragon fruit, groundnut) for farmers in Purulia and the Sundarbans; business training and help with licences and loans for small entrepreneurs. Our judgment 10%, 0 to 30%.

rows.label: Years a supported farm or business keeps its higher income
rows.explainer: Seeds and training raise a season's harvest; new crops and businesses can keep paying: our judgment 3 years, 1 (one season's inputs) to 6 (a dragon-fruit orchard or a lasting business).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, farming and business support
rows.explainer: The annual report gives case studies only, no comparison group, and farmers who join may be those who would have done well anyway: our judgment 0.6, 0.3 (gains mostly selection) to 0.9 (gains as judged).

rows.label: Missing-data step, farming and business support
rows.explainer: Thin: reach and effect are judgments.

rows.label: Units of value from farming and business support
rows.formula: fa_households * @household_size.india * ln(1 + fa_income_gain) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, fa_years) * $uov_per_ln_consumption * fa_evidence_adj * fa_missing_data_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount

rows.label: Households enrolled a year in Bihar's Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana

source.title: J-PAL, 'Government of Bihar, JEEViKA and J-PAL South Asia present impact evaluation findings of Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana', 16 October 2026
source.quote: As of April 2026, SJY has reached 210,218 households across all 38 districts of Bihar

rows.explainer: The Government of Bihar's graduation programme, launched in 2018, targets 200,000 ultra-poor households (annual report p. 13) and had enrolled 210,218 by April 2026 (J-PAL's update of 16 October 2026): about 26,000 a year. Our judgment 25,000, 10,000 to 45,000.

rows.label: Government spending on the programme a year (rupees)
rows.explainer: A budget of ₹840 crore (annual report p. 13; the Bihar paper p. 6: INR 8,400 million) over about seven years of enrolment: ₹120 crore a year, ₹60 to 200 crore.

rows.label: Bandhan-Konnagar's share of the resources behind the programme
rows.explainer: Its technical team's cost over its cost plus the government's (Convention 2): about 2%.

rows.label: Consumption gain per household, Bihar trial

source.title: Banerjee, Duflo, Orduña Correcher, Mukhopadhyay, Sabarwal and Sharan, 'Does the Graduation Program Scale? Evidence from India', working paper, 19 October 2026
source.quote: Across both endlines, per capita monthly consumption rises by 0.38–0.44 SD (27–29%) over the control mean

rows.explainer: Intention to treat, two and three years after the asset; 20% to 35%.

rows.label: Years Bihar graduation households keep their consumption gain
rows.explainer: Measured to three years; the West Bengal trial's gain held to ten. Our judgment 8 years, 3 to 15.

rows.label: Missing-data step, Bihar technical assistance
rows.explainer: Thin: the reach is a judgment and Bandhan-Konnagar's part is technical help to a government programme, which no trial isolates.

rows.label: Units of value from technical assistance to Bihar's programme
rows.formula: sj_households * household_size * ln(1 + sj_gain) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, sj_years) * $uov_per_ln_consumption * sj_credit_share * sj_missing_data_adj * leverage_funging_adj * wait_discount
rows.explainer: Households × people per household (the same ultra-poor women-headed households as Bandhan-Konnagar's own) × the trial's gain over its years × Bandhan-Konnagar's share of the resources.
